narrative.summaryIntro:
Banke Bihari Temple in Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, houses a black stone murti worshipped as the combined form of Radha and Krishna, standing in the tribhanga (three-fold bent) posture. The temple is one of Vrindavan's most visited Krishna shrines and is known for its distinctive darshan practice: rather than remaining continuously open to view, a curtain before the deity is repeatedly drawn and reopened through the day. No bells are rung inside the temple, in keeping with the deity's worship in a child-like form.

The temple registers among the highest daily footfalls of any Vrindavan shrine, with reported figures of 30,000–40,000 devotees a day, rising to several lakh on festivals such as Janmashtami. Crowd safety at the temple has drawn government and judicial attention in recent years.
narrative.documentedHistory:
According to the temple's own account, the ascetic and musician Swami Haridas (traditionally dated to the 16th century) worshipped a murti under the name Kunj Bihari at Nidhivan, a forest grove in Vrindavan associated with his devotional practice. Temple tradition holds that the deity — a combined form of Radha and Krishna — was revealed to Haridas and passed into the care of his principal disciple, Goswami Jagannath, whose descendants, the Goswami sevayats, continue to conduct its worship, including three daily ceremonies: Shringar (morning adornment), Rajbhog (midday offering) and Shayan (evening rest).

Following disputes in the 19th century among different groups of Haridas's followers, the deity was moved from Nidhivan to a newly built temple nearby, completed around 1862–1864 in Rajasthani architectural style. The Mathura district government's tourism page places the temple among several major Vrindavan shrines, including the nearby Radhavallabh and Govind Dev temples.

In the 21st century the temple has drawn government and judicial attention over crowd safety: a stampede occurred at the temple in 2022, and on 15 May 2025 the Supreme Court of India permitted the Uttar Pradesh government to use funds from the temple trust (reported as up to ₹500 crore) to acquire about five acres of adjoining land for a devotee holding area and corridor project, with the acquired land to be registered in the deity's name. Administration of the temple's funds and the corridor project were the subject of continuing litigation and government measures as of the sources consulted here, and details should be treated as subject to change.

visitingInfo.officialContactNote: The temple registers among the highest daily footfalls in Vrindavan (reported at 30,000–40,000 devotees a day, rising to several lakh on festivals such as Janmashtami), and a Supreme Court-directed corridor and crowd-management project was under way as of May 2025. Confirm current darshan arrangements before travelling, especially around major festivals. Address: Goda Vihar, Madan Mohan Bankey Bihari Road, Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh 281121.

festivals.significance: Krishna's birthday; among the temple's major festivals and its highest-footfall day.
Birthday of Radha and, per the temple's own site, also observed as the birthday of Swami Haridas. Listed by the temple for 19 September in 2026; the exact date shifts yearly with the lunar calendar.
Maha Raas celebration; the deity is shown holding a flute for this festival. Listed by the temple for 26 October in 2026.
